utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Lukic or Mr. Ivetic -- probably Mr. Ivetic I think, are you able to advise us further in relation to the six PJP commanders anonymously listed on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that we have sent out an e-mail identifying the names and the exact unit or detachment that they were commanders of last night, so hopefully that should address all six of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you do have the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In a moment the cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will continue. Please remember what I said yesterday morning, that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence start to finish. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yesterday we were discussing your relationship with the MUP, and I would like to briefly continue with that by looking at document P2014. This is an order that you have been shown quite a few times. It's an order in relation to the Drenica operation on the 25th of May. I take it that you drafted this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the last page, please, then I'll be able to tell you who made this. Yes, indeed, I'm one of the persons who were involved in drafting this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, you were the -- you see on the front page there it says: "To the command of the MUP." I take it that you wrote that as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write that myself but it was written by someone in the organ for operations and affairs. The MUP is hereby called upon to use one of its units to participate in this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To whom was this document sent? To whom in the MUP was the document sent?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific right now whether it was actually delivered to someone in person or whether someone was informed. This was normally done by my deputy. Once the planning stage had been completed he would take it upon himself to inform all those who were involved in an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, who in the MUP did you intend to receive this?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was meant to be like this: Someone from the MUP was to be informed, and then this person was to inform his own unit of the fact that an action had been planned, and then there would be coordination at the tactical level between the brigade and the PJP detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not simply someone. This is: "To the command of the MUP." Who did you intend to receive it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sir, it was someone who was in the MUP staff who was in charge of planning who was supposed to receive this, and all this business about actions and about the involvement of units of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: See, I'm sorry if I'm pressing because we -- with these questions. Many of the questions I ask, I ask because General Lazarevic indicated that you would be the one to know, and now you are telling me you don't know who was the commander of the MUP that this document was intended for. Very well. And you don't know where this command of the MUP was located?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, they do not have a command as such, but here it was also done for the unit commands, the brigades. So they have an HQ, they have their leaders, but their something [as interpreted] was in the general Pristina area. I don't know where exactly they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've heard of a body called the MUP staff for Kosovo based in Pristina. Do you know of that body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know who was head of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, on the face of it this would be intended for him, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, his staff, maybe not personally, but his staff, his unit that was going about this business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the 3rd Army were to send a document like this to the Pristina Corps, who would it be intended to go to at the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an established procedure in the army, when mail is received, checked, if there was a document being sent by the army command to the corps command, this would have been received in an office, checked, and forwarded to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who would be regarded as responsible, ultimately responsible, in the Pristina Corps for complying with the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For receiving the order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For complying with the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most responsible person in that command would have been in charge with complying with that order, implementing that order and any other order that was received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't try to confuse the situation with language. Who in the Pristina Corps would be ultimately responsible for complying with the order, according to the principle of singleness or unity of command, which has been emphasised by soldier after soldier here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked - if I could move on - a significant amount of question about your -- about the VJ's subordination or non-resubordination of the MUP during combat operations. I don't intend to ask -- go through this again but to ask you one thing: You said that many times the VJ provided artillery support but it would only be for units within the combat disposition of the VJ artillery units. What do you mean when you say "combat disposition"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the combat disposition of a unit, what we mean is where forces are positioned, firing positions, support, observation posts, command posts at a high level also the forces and equipment that take up these areas and sectors, that's what we mean when we say "combat disposition."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have seen in many of the operations that we have had evidence about -- or actions that we have had evidence about MUP units requiring VJ fire support and being within the combat disposition of the MUP -- of the VJ. I would like to ask you a hypothetical question. Should something unexpected happen in any of these operations where the VJ is blocking territory and providing fire support and the MUP is confronting the KLA and it required an immediate decision, who would prevail if there was disagreement amongst the persons in what you call the combined command or the Joint Command that was leading this operation? Which single person would prevail and make the decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this combined command post, there are no superiors or subordinates. All the representatives of the various commands are equal, each in command of their unit. There are no distinctions. Everyone has their own chain of command and they're all equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What if an unexpected situation, for example, a KLA unit turned out to be stronger than expected and turned around and attacked VJ and MUP units, endangering VJ personnel and MUP personnel, that's the lives of these persons, and then a decision had to be made, would someone have the responsibility to make that ultimate decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, that certainly wouldn't be my understanding. For example, MUP unit is attacked, is facing problems that it can't deal with on its own, it would send a request to an army commander, the commander of an army unit, to lend some support, for example, firing support, to give them support with a specific problem that may have occurred during an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What if there was no agreement, wouldn't Article 7 of the Law of Defence apply? That is, a senior VJ person there would have to take command -- Article 17.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I don't know that at any point throughout the war there was any misunderstanding about this. There was always a lot of mutual understanding and support between the VJ and the MUP, so I can't speak hypothetically about this simply because it's meaningless unless there is a particular action that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you don't know throughout any point in the war there was any misunderstanding about this, you mean, are you saying you don't know through the war that there was any disagreement between the VJ and the MUP in these joint combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's a much broader question, the one you're asking me now. I'm just focusing on a situation in which a problem occurs. Now, how do they go about this? There is a request for support at a certain point in time in order to overcome this problem and continue an action in a successful manner. There was no reason for any misunderstandings to occur between the two because they each had their own chain of command, and that's how they were working, autonomously each along their own axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene here. Just, General, I shall feel grateful if you kindly answer my question. But you appreciate the relevance of Article 17 of the Law of Defence in case such a situation arises, although I'm quite astonished to see that such a situation will never arise; after all, they are human beings, there is human nature involved. But let's concentrate on the relevance of Article 17. You agree with what is said in Article 17, will that emerge? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what I'm saying. In practice this never happened throughout the war. Therefore, I can't speak about Article 17 of the Law on Defence in terms of whether it was applied or when. There was no need to apply that particular article. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us about the Drenica action which had to be replanned. Apart from that situation, apart from that Drenica action, do you know of any other situations where an operation or an action had to be completely replanned, as occurred in the Drenica situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, as far as I can remember, there were some actions that had to be replanned because of overspill by certain terrorist forces, so one had to go back to certain areas and re-plan things, and it's Drenica that I have in mind above all and I don't mean Mount Drenica, I mean the Drenica area, the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of any other action or operation that had to be replanned because of problems with the MUP in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, I can't remember right now. If there's a document that I could use to jog my memory -- as I am, I don't think I can possibly remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you P1468 and I think I showed you the wrong part of this. I would like to show you that document again and ask you a question about it, and this is to move on to another topic. And if we could go straight -- these are the notes I showed you yesterday of the -- of meetings of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go straight to page 137 of the B/C/S and page 151 of the English. Well, we don't need to go to the English, actually, if we could just go to page 137 of the B/C/S. So if we could have page 137 of the B/C/S on one page and page 136 of the B/C/S. Could we have page 136 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 136 is a note or the notes for the 13th -- for the 14th of October, 1998, and that's on your right and page 137 on your left is the notes for the 21st of October, 1998. You can see that the writings are different, the penmanship is not the same. Now, what I asked you about yesterday is the one on your right, the first one, the earlier one. I want to ask you about the one on your left. Do you recognise the writing?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, I can't distinguish. I can only confirm what you suggested. It is obvious that the two samples were made by two different hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The one on your left, is this not the writing of your assistant, Jesevic -- I may have the name correct, Jeftovic -- sorry, Jesevic --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Tesevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I'm not sure whether this is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Just a couple of questions. The air corps of the VJ was operational during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, at the beginning of the war but not any later than that because there was no way for it to resist or stand up to a far superior aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Up until when?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain because I don't know anything reliable about it, but perhaps the first couple of days, from the beginning of the aggression I reckon up until the end of March, but certainly not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also spoke about units being brought into Kosovo from outside Kosovo shortly before the war.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, esteemed Prosecutor. Pursuant to orders from the General Staff and the 3rd Army command, some of the units were brought to Kosovo and Metohija, specifically Combat Group 37 from the 37th Motorised Brigade of the Uzice Corps of the 2nd Army, BG-252 or to be more precise, the mechanised battalion of the 252nd Armoured Brigade from the 1st Army; and DO, a Combat Group from the 72nd Special Brigade, about 100 men from the Nis Corps BG-21, the equivalent of a battalion, a combat group. I apologise, there was also TG-211 from the 211th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are aware that bringing these units into Kosovo at that time would have been in breach of the October Agreement in respect to the OSCE monitoring missions?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, as far as I know, no unit outside the Pristina Corps was brought there without the approval of the General Staff or the 3rd Army command without notifying the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the months of February and March of 1999 in your preparations for combat in spring, did you contemplate that the KVM monitoring mission would remain in Kosovo should NATO intervene?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, truth be told, that wasn't my job; I didn't spend any time thinking about that. I was in no position to assess whether it would still be there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You prepared P2809 [sic]. That is a Pristina Corps order the 15th of February which covered many of the operations that were conducted, particularly during the early part of the war, late March. And in the order for those operations, did you not contemplate --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it's an erroneous reference to the document

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, counsel, it's P2808, not P2809.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In making these plans - and this is one that you drafted - did you and the other senior leaders of the VJ not contemplate operations to jam the communications of the KVM or the OSCE monitors?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honourable Prosecutor, that is not right at all. Allow me to explain. This order to crush and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the region of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo stemmed from the order of the command of the 3rd Army, if I'm not mistaken, from the 27th or 28th of January, where a task was given to plan anti-terrorist actions for the mentioned areas, and especially due to the build-up of NATO forces in Macedonia, specifically the multi-national brigade of NATO. This area of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo are areas that are suitable for landing, and the planned action was to prevent a landing of the mentioned multi-national brigade of NATO to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at page 27 of this order because I think -- I see from your answer here you are telling me it's not right to say that you contemplated operations to jam the communications of the OSCE monitors. Page 27 in English and that's page 10 to 11, the paragraph that starts at page 10 and ends on page 11 in B/C/S. And while we are getting there, can I indicate that it is 2808. I notice that the transcript indicates P2828. It's P2808. It indicates that you should conduct electronic jamming in accordance with a special order and carry out electronic deception by breaking into the communication systems of, among others, the OSCE verification mission. So contrary to what you are saying, it is true, isn't it, that in carrying out these operations against the KLA you intended to interfere with the communications of the OSCE, who was supposed to be monitoring your operations.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says basically in this paragraph, electronic warfare. First of all, one should take measures against the Siptar terrorist forces and what is coming from the Republic of Macedonia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't any -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just focusing on the OSCE mission for the time being. It is clear, sir, it is true that you did not want the OSCE monitors to know what you were doing in these operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honourable Prosecutor, as far as I know, the OSCE mission was allowed and enabled to have a look at every unit, every position, all the armaments, everything in every one of our units and everything that they were interested in, all units, all sectors, et cetera. If you allow me to say, during 1998 I was commander in Gnjilane, I was commander of a brigade, and several times they came to see me and I made it possible for them to see everything that they had asked to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe that is all I have, if I may just check my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is all I have for this witness. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we will start with what we heard about last, 28085 [as interpreted]. Could we please have a look at that, or rather, 2808. Page 10, please, the one that we saw previously, and immediately after that, page 11. In the Serbian version page 10, please. Mr. Stamp showed you this sentence: "Electronic jamming should be carried out according to a special order ..." Was readiness envisaged for that or did this require a special order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As stated here, in accordance with a special order, what was supposed to follow was a new special order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did a special order on jamming ever follow?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information to the effect that the OSCE mission was submitting information about your positions to the NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had such information. They used GPS systems to locate various sites and facilities, which was later confirmed during the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I can only say many times these -- what I think is a grossly leading question is asked and answered even before one can react. So if I can just ask if counsel wants to explore some territory, he should try to keep the questions as open as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Bakrac, you have to bear that in mind, that the answer we've just heard is pretty valueless in view of the terms of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just read what is written there and then I asked whether there was a special order. That is what is written in this text. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what the objection is to, Mr. Bakrac. The objection is to the question at line 17: "Did you have any information to the effect that the OSCE mission was submitting information about your positions to the NATO forces?" What you should have asked was: Can you think of any reason why that provision was included in P2808? And then we would have had the benefit of his spontaneous recollection, which would have been valuable evidence. As it is, you've devalued the evidence that he's given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. We had evidence about that. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are determined to have the last word on this, Mr. Bakrac, which ill-becomes you in these circumstances. But if we have plenty of other evidence on it, why on earth are you asking this witness? Just please get on with it and deal with it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, a question was put to you about Article 17 of the Law on Defence, and if I'm not mistaken what it says there is that MUP organs may be resubordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia. I would be interested in the following, since a hypothetical question was put to you, who has the last say? If there is resubordination, is that situation different, if there is no resubordination or if there's only coordination, rather?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a situation if there were no resubordination, then everything is clear, then there are relations of command involved and then there is no further dilemma with regard to other tasks and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My friend Mr. Stamp asked you on page 10, lines 14 through 16, while preparing the spring offensive, did you think that the OSCE would remain in Kosovo. My question was: Were you preparing a spring offensive?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; on the contrary. We were getting ready to thwart the spring offensive of the Siptar terrorist forces. That was one of the tasks of the command of the 3rd Army, or rather, the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stefanovic. Yesterday my colleague Mr. Ivetic asked you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one -- before you move on. Are you referring to the question at line 14 on page 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 10, 14 through 16, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English question does not suggest that the VJ were preparing a spring offensive. The question was: "In your preparations for combat in the spring ..." which Is consistent with what we understood the position to be, the intention that there would be a spring offensive and to resist it. However, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, so what was shown to you was PD84 [as interpreted], the combat report of the command of the Pristina Corps, and you were asked about mixed check-points or joint check-points. Could we have a look at 5D376, please, and could we have a look at paragraph 1. 376. Could you have a look at the first paragraph, please, and could you give me your comments. This is a document of the Ministry of the Interior dated the 13th of May, 1999. And does it pertain to the setting up of joint check-points?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order to deal with looting, et cetera -- should I read this out or should I just give you my comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just give us your comments. We can read it for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of an agreement of the MUP and the commander of the Pristina Corps, joint check-points were set up and patrols with a basic joint task -- so the members of the army should stop and check VJ members in vehicles while MUP members should stop and check MUP members and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, since we are talking about the 13th of May, you read this on the basis of an agreement between the head of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija and the commander of the Pristina Corps of the Army of Yugoslavia. Could there have been an agreement at all or would it have been resolved differently had there been resubordination?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say once again, if there is resubordination then there is no more functional relationship of discussion, agreement; there is subordination, there is singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yesterday you were asked about another document dated the 25th of April, and you said that it was an attempt to operationalize that order, and you wanted us to look at the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then please have P1722, that's an order from the 3rd Army command issued pursuant to an order from the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And could you please look at the first paragraph, and if you could please comment and tell us whether this is the order that you were talking about that you said it had been impossible to implement and that you had actually attempted to operationalize.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the basic -- the original order regulating the resubordination of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And in this order -- is the order issued only the effect that the units should be resubordinated or is there more to it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the units and organs of the interior for the purpose of having singleness of command in the execution of combat missions, so everything is affected, units and organs. Although this is perhaps not phrased in the most fortunate manner because the secretariats are organs too, but the overall resubordination is what is meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now when we're talking about the resubordination, does resubordination mean that only offensive operations, anti-terrorist actions are to be carried out or does it also entail something else?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking about this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm asking a general question, not relating to this order, but what does resubordination entail, only execution of offensive anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please give me a minute so that I can be as specific as possible. After this order was issued, it was unclear to either party how they should proceed. So after a few days at the corps command, we put together and issued another order dated the 25th of April, where we tried to be as precise and as specific as possible, so that only that the police units may be employed only from time to time in certain actions fighting the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you explained all that. What I am interested in is whether resubordination, generally speaking, entails only the ad hoc actions or something else too.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure. Could you be more specific. Are you talking about the work in general or just combat actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, what other kinds of work would resubordination entail?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if an element or if a unit is resubordinated to a command, then it is under an obligation to report to that command regularly on its activities after some actions are carried out, to brief the command, to report, to be in contact. So it is a complex activity. It is not just you resubordinate somebody and that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All that you said, does this entail also the combat control of the territory holding the axes that were taken, undertaking ambushes and raids?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. If we're talking about combat actions, not all the forces in a unit would attack to rout and destroy. There was some units that would block some positions, hold certain sectors, ensure that the roads were passable, provide support. So this entails all those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I've missed something in your earlier evidence from what Mr. Bakrac is saying. Mr. Bakrac, what is the exhibit number for the order of the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please be given just a moment. I have it here. Your Honour, that's P2809, so it's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see that one, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may assist, in the preamble there is a reference to the document that we've just looked at dated the 20th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The part that I think -- well, I appear to have missed from what Mr. Bakrac was saying is when you apparently have told us before that after the 20th of April order was issued it was unclear to either party how they should proceed. Now, how were you aware that the position was unclear to both the MUP and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in contacts at the corps command that was definitely so, in contact with the various organs in the corps command and also in the contacts with the MUP representatives, who were saying, How should we implement this? So these were just talks, conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is -- these are conversations you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, and the other organs of the command, the corps commander informed us about it. I mean the organs of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But tell me, who was the most senior MUP person? Give me a name that you spoke to and who discussed with you, How should we implement this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I talked with the commanders of the police units, in light of the fact that we carried out those actions, so I was in quite frequent contact with them. But as for the officers in the staff, I really didn't have an opportunity to discuss this with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, give me the name of a person that you discussed this with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I remember that I talked with Colonel Brakovic several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is difficult about the order and how to implement it, paragraph 1? Where's the difficulty? It's in such simple, clear terms, where is the difficulty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise. We're now not talking about this order, we're talking about the previous order. This order is an attempt to provide some specific guide-lines as to how this could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the situation between the 20th of April and the 25th, and you have already told us - and apparently you told us earlier and I have missed it - that it was unclear to either party how they should proceed. Now, I would like to know what it was the MUP people you talked to after the 20th of April and before the 25th of April said was difficult about implementing this 20th of April order. I want meat on the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are two reasons. The first basic reason is that MUP did not receive any orders from the ministry, from their superiors, about this resubordination; and second, if you allow me, second, it was not clear, this initial order was not clear as to what should be resubordinated and what shouldn't be. What methodology should be applied for this resubordination if it ever occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first reason you give is a quite different reason from the one that you're giving at the moment. So let's lay that aside. We've heard it before, we know that that's the main theme for the non-effect of this order. But on the second point, it was not clear as to what should be resubordinated. It couldn't be clearer, Mr. Stefanovic. "The units and agencies of internal affairs shall be resubordinated to the Pristina Corps and Nis Corps in the execution of combat missions." Now, what's difficult to understand about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the difficulty lay now -- that we discussed in our conversations is whether the services in the secretariats issuing passports, controlling traffic, and so on, I'm not familiar with their organs, their services, whether all that should be resubordinated to the army. So that was the essential problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are these part of combat operations? I mean -- combat missions? This is simple language we're talking about here. I mean, these are obviously not part of a combat mission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, absolutely. That's not a combat element at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me, was there a power struggle between the VJ and the MUP at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, I didn't know that. I was not aware of that and I don't think that there were any misunderstandings in -- that there was no struggle, as you're talking about. There was just this stand that they took that there was no order on resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate matter, Mr. Stefanovic. That's not the explanation you've given today for this difficulty, and I'm trying to find out what was the specific nature of the problem that the MUP officials you spoke to saw in implementing this order and I've yet to hear any from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me try and do that once again, to be quite specific. They considered that the overall, the -- all of the organs and services of the police could not be resubordinated to the army because it was simply impossible. It was unclear how this could be done at all. So that's where the problem was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this was never discussed, as far as you are aware, above the level of unit commanders of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no. I didn't know whether anyone discussed that at a higher level, when or indeed what might have been discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you told us in your examination-in-chief yesterday, or rather, the day before yesterday, you gave us names of people that you coordinated with in planning actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P1811.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is a document from the Ministry of the Interior. You see in front of you the decision to establish a ministry staff for fighting terrorism. It is dated May 1999, and we can see here Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Arsenijevic. Is this the person that you were referring to that you said that you had --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the police officer Milenko Arsenijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at page 2 of this document. And could we look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were asked by my colleague Mr. Ivetic about the planning, whether you did any planning for the MUP and so on. Now, was one of the tasks of the staff, as envisaged in item 2, to plan, organize, and manage the work and the -- to employ the organizational units of the ministry and the units attached to it in their engagement on the suppression of terrorism in the territory of the -- of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what this article says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So who is doing the planning for the units of the Ministry of the Interior, as far as their actions were concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think the other question was okay but this question goes a little bit too far without showing a foundation for how this witness would know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Mr. -- Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, if you look at paragraph 3 -- if we look at paragraph 3 as far as the work of the staff is concerned, who is the head of staff responsible to for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way it reads here, to the minister whom he reports to on everything that done, any measures taken and any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You were asked yesterday about some maps, some questions about some maps by Mr. Ivetic. We see that the axes of the MUP and the positions of the MUP were marked on those maps as well as the positions of the VJ. Were any other positions marked on those maps, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were decision maps, diagrams, and only the VJ, the MUP, support units, and neighbours were marked on those maps, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, that is the paramount thing, isn't it, in terms of planning? You can't plan without knowing where the enemy is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you plan also in relation to the Kosovo Liberation Army, since you actually marked them on your maps?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- well, it's impossible, simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, sir, can we please have P2591. This is an exhibit that Mr. Stamp was showing you. This is entitled: "Analysis of the 37th Motorised Brigade," which is a brigade that you discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at general weaknesses and flaws and then there are these bullets, number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see that it says: "According to our assessment in Kosmac and Cicavica, the number of the units and men involved in relation to the results that were achieved was not adequate, or rather, the activities covered a large area with relatively negligible effects in terms of crushing the Siptar terrorist forces." So my question if we look at this particular bullet point and the analysis, you have large-scale forces and negligible effects in terms of destroying the Siptar terrorist forces. Would that be an example of disproportionate use of force?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you could term it that way and I don't think that is actually what is being implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How would you interpret that, large-scale forces and a minor effect?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of different factors that affect this situation, it's a very complex area, it's a wooded area. The enemy's familiar with the ground. They are fortifying their positions. They are using guerilla tactics and it's very difficult to crush and destroy terrorism. We've known that for a long time and unfortunately this is proving true now again over the last couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I only have a couple of questions left for my re-examination. Mr. Stamp showed you P2808 and the register number was 455-1 or the file number. And he asked you about the register and about the topics that were covered and whether each topic was assigned a number. My question: 411 [as interpreted], is that exclusively in relation to fighting the Siptar terrorists or were there other documents that were covered by that number?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other documents that were covered by that number too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about this file number? If we look at the number, can we tell immediately which organ is in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, each organ at the corps command had a certain number of documents and these registers and numbers that went with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I said 455 to you, which organ would that be?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the operations organ in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Speaking of this document, P2808, in order to dash right through it, I don't think there's any need for us to bring it back on the screen. I'll ask you a very simple question. What about this clause about armed non-Siptar population, where was that taken from in order to be used in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by the Pristina Corps commander and this clause in paragraph 2, tasks for the corps, was taken from an order by the 3rd Army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you allowed to change that clause in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: More about that, 5D1284, our next exhibit. First of all, item 2, paragraph 2. Paragraph 2, it says "tasks," or rather, "task." Can you please read the first sentence and tell me whether this, in fact, shows that there is resubordination or perhaps something else.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 243rd Mechanised Brigade with BG 2.2, Combat Group 2.2, Combat Group 21, the 57th Border Battalion without the 2nd Border Company, the 60th Military Territorial Detachment Vitina and a Fagot anti-tank guided missile system battery shall take up positions in the area of responsibility and organize defence of the following task: In coordinated action with the 175th Infantry Brigade and 549th Motorised Brigade and armed non-Siptar population through decisive defence of the state border, prevent raids of NATO forces along the following axes ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does this not show that this armed non-Siptar population was, in fact, resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, it's just another series of leading questions, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I meant no ill. I really didn't. I have two more questions left. I will do my best to make my next question a not-leading one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at 8.4, page 9, and please tell us what the abbreviation stands for. The top of the page, please, 8.4. There is an abbreviation there. Can you please tell us what it means.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 8.4 we see an abbreviation, that's right, and its expansion would be: Anti-nuclear, chemical, biological security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Now my question: Who in the defence ministry would be looking into issues to do with decontamination, which particular body?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil protection, forces of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now 5D300, please. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 2 displayed as well. This is the federal defence ministry, local organ, Pristina defence administration. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It says head of administration, Petar Ilic. Do you know and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was administration head for defence, organ of the federal defence ministry, in Pristina, yes, that's right, administration head in Pristina, which is in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which forces was he in charge of?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of civil protection and civil defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to save time, we also have 5D301, corroborating this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my question is this: These civil protection, civil defence units are units of the defence ministry. Who was in charge of arming them and who was in command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal defence ministry was in charge of that, and they were their superiors through their own local organs, branch offices, administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. My very last question is related to 3049, it's a document, P, P, it's an OTP document, P3049. My learned friend Mr. Stamp yesterday was showing you paragraph 3 and he put something to you about this armed non-Siptar population. He suggested that this was a minor action to lift the blockade of a road. We're waiting for the document to turn up. Can you please look at paragraphs 3 and 4 and tell me whether this is just about lifting the blockade of a particular road or is this a more comprehensive action. Paragraph 3: "I hereby decide ..." Please, paragraph 3 and 4 of item 3: "I hereby decide ..." So what Mr. Stamp said, this was only about lifting the blockade of a certain road, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I did not say that's only about lifting a blockade. I said the primary task was to clear a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, that's it, I suppose. General, sir, Mr. Stamp has just put in a reaction. Can you tell us whether clearing the road was, in fact, the primary task.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can tell if you look at this that stage 1 is supposed to go on for one day, crush the Siptar terrorist forces in Lebane village-Glavnik village, Prvi Tunnel-Stari Trg, and in the following sectors Cica Glava, Carevica, Vasiljevo, and the next task would be to clear the road and get to the line Gornje Prekaze-Prelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. If we could please go back to the previous page. General, is there any assignment that is being given to the Pristina Corps in item 2?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't see any in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that the reason why we don't see the phrase "armed non-Siptar population" here?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It should not go unsaid that you ended as you began on yet another leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, when it came to issuing weapons to the civil defence and civil protection, where were these weapons issued from; in other words, where were they stored?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're looking at forces of the federal defence ministry, civil protection and civil defence units and local offices of the ministry were in charge of providing weapons for them and I'm sure these weapons were stored in storages or warehouses, storage facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Controlled by the Ministry of Defence or controlled by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Your Honour, this was under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your evidence is that the Ministry of Defence had a stockpile of weapons to issue to people in civil defence and civil protection?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand it's their responsibility from your evidence. I just want to be absolutely clear that they also had physical control over the weapons before they were issued.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant. Physical control, they certainly did not have. They certainly didn't have forces to provide security for the warehouses, but the weapons were theirs and under their control. As for physically where they were in some storage facility, that I cannot say at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know, my first question to you on this subject was: "When it came to issuing weapons to the civil defence and civil protection, where were these weapons issued from; in other words, where were they stored?"

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, in the storage facilities where military equipment and weapons are stored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And my next question was: "Controlled by the Ministry of Defence or controlled by the VJ?" Now, it's a very simple question, and your answer was: " ... this was under their control," which meant I had to go further. Now, for the avoidance of any doubt on this subject: Under whose control were the weapons, under whose physical control were the weapons before they were issued to members of civil defence and civil protection?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, it was in separate facilities, facilities that were singled out. It was under the physical control of the army and the police probably -- well, it couldn't be anybody else, they don't have physically the forces to provide security for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how did the police come to have any involvement in this?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't quite clear. Maybe they had something in their warehouses too. I'm talking about the army. I don't know what the situation was in the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a translation problem, but if it is I'm surprised that no one has leapt up to tell me. Your answer is recorded in English as: "It was under the physical control of the army and the police probably," and that's why I asked you how the police come into this. Now, can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKO STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I said "probably." I'm not sure about that. Maybe, maybe yes, maybe no. I do apologise. I wasn't very specific on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was our last witness, and we hereby complete our evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As in the other cases, I think subject to tidying up the situation in relation to exhibits, and you will require to review your exhibits and submit one final motion for admission of any outstanding exhibits from the bar table for us to consider. Now, when will you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will do that as soon as possible. I will look into this with our assistants. You know why? Because we need to check what the situation is with untranslated exhibits, and when I receive information on that I will address you - of course if you allow me to - in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think at this stage we need to have a specific time for you to submit this motion, and it should be submitted even if certain exhibits have not been translated and you can make clear which ones have not been translated and you can then file each as it is translated. We will of course take account of how long that takes. It's -- there's no open-ended provision here for you to arrive with your translations; they have to be done pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, experience has taught me that it's better for you to give me a dead-line rather than to have me set a dead-line for myself, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, somebody's learned something from this trial. That dead-line then will be the end of next week, and even if an item is not translated it must be included in that. You have this one final opportunity, and one only, to submit documents that you wish us to consider. The reason that the end of next week is of some significance is because we've also instructed Mr. Visnjic to get his translations sorted out by then as well so that we can spend some time resolving this now when we have time, rather than later when we will not have so much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. At least for once I was right, I would have given a shorter dead-line. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we note that the case for the fifth accused rests, subject to a motion for admission of exhibits from the bar table, which will be submitted by next Friday, which is the 15th of February. I think the best plan now is that we take the break at this stage and we resume at 11.00 -- oh, sorry, yes, my mistake. We will resume, yes, at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before the presentation of evidence begins, Mr. Lukic, there is one matter that we've been discussing which I would like you to give some thought to. In the case of each of the other accused, we've allowed time after the close of their evidence to tender exhibits to tidy things up. Now, it may well be at the end of your case there will be some exhibits, that that situation will be unavoidable, but for the vast majority of your exhibits it should be possible to have them tendered to us much earlier than that. The reason in your case is obvious, because we are -- we are anxious to get to the point of decision-making as soon as possible in the interests of everyone. We do not want people in custody unnecessarily, and therefore our objective is to be as expeditious as is consistent with fairness. So we will invite you to give some indication a bit later on about how much time you would need to tender a comprehensive motion if you are intending to do so, and we will make an order about that. It's not of immediate concern, and therefore we can get on with the evidence just now, but sometime before the end of this month I think the position should be made clear to all concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So who is your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our first witness is Dragan Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need one clarification from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the witness starts. We provided this witness with a binder of documents - there is nothing written on those documents - if something goes wrong with the system, and if you think that he shouldn't be using that, I mean hard copies, we should advise the witness not to or whatever you decide, but we provide -- we think that it's -- sometimes can speed up the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with you entirely, I see no problem with that, as long as they are clean copies identical to what's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful, it actually even avoids the interruption when the usher has to transport the documents across the courtroom. It's a helpful move. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. -- oh, no, we're not at the afternoon yet. Good morning, Mr. Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. May I start now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic, counsel for the accused Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please state your name for the record and could you tell us briefly about your career.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Paunovic. I was born on the 12th of November, 1970, in Kraljevo, the Republic of Serbia. I completed the secondary police school, and I've been a member of the Ministry of the Interior since the 3rd of July, 1989. I had different duties within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, and I would like to point out some more significant ones. I was deployed in the police administration of the Ministry of the Interior on the 1st of November, 1998, and I was assigned chief of the secretariat of the Ministry of the Interior in Kraljevo on the 27th of February, 2001, and I held that position until November 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please call up in e-court P1508.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we're waiting, you have it in front of you. Tell us, please, when did you join the PJP units of the milicija, which later became the PJP units of the "policija," police, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: As for the PJP, I first joined them in 1993, which coincides with the actual establishment of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you now please have a look at this exhibit, P1508.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of a document is this, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: We see a here document a which was called basis for the formation of special police units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the document is dated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of August, 1993, and it was adopted by the Ministry of the Interior, the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2 under (b) we have a heading: "Purpose, tasks, conditions, and mode of use of PJMs." Could you tell us what these basic tasks are, these basic security tasks conducted by the PJMs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: As for the members of the special police units, professional and responsible members of the police were selected for these units, those who had outstanding professional capabilities. Their age was up to 35, or rather, up to the age of 45 for officers. Tasks of the members of the PJMs were numerous, and I am particularly going to refer to the ones mentioned here which fully reflected the nature and role that they had at the time. What I can particularly highlight on the basis of my experience is the engagement of special police units in maintaining stable public order and dealing with any disruptions in public order. Number 2, bring into custody persons who are crime suspects, and when there is a danger that they will use fire-arms and endanger innocent civilians, that is to say, other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude -- and the other tasks as envisaged in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These parts of the police, were they specially trained in comparison to the regular police force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the fact that they were chosen on the basis of their high moral and professional qualities, members of the PJMs, or rather, PJPs were also trained for different types of activities that they undertook. They were particularly trained for situations when there were disruptions in public law and order, situations that had to do with bringing into custody dangerous crime suspects, and exercising control over situations where there was a danger of threats of sabotage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at 3 -- page 3 under (v) now, control and command, in PJMs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there some subtle distinction between the initials PJP and PJM?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning it was milicija, that's what's M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so the units remained the same and the title changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, you heard what His Honour was interested in. Was it just the name that changed? Did everything else remain the same functionally and structurally when the name was changed from milicija, police into policija, police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the same in terms of their characteristic and tasks and function, these were the same units; the only thing that was changed was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this happened sometime in 1995 or 1996, but I'm not entirely certain about the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time did the overall structure of the MUP change its name from milicija to policija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your answer to that question? It was missed by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. The answer was: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you to go to the section marked as (v), control and command, that's page 3, in the PJM.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English it's (c) because it's alphabetic discrepancy. In Cyrillic, v comes after b; in Latin, c.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paunovic, who was in a position to order PJP or PJM units to be assembled and to get involved on a task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: As for the assembling of PJP units, or rather, issuing an order for their involvement, this was under the exclusive jurisdiction of the minister of the interior or another person authorised by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is in command of PJP units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: PJP units or detachments of those PJP units were under the command of detachment commanders of these PJP units and officers of lower-ranking units within those detachments, lower ranking in terms of organization, for example, companies. PJP detachment commanders were responsible to PJP commanders [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, it was misrecorded, the plural was used in the other part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please again say who the PJP detachment commanders were responsible to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: The commanders of PJP detachments, which implies that there were more of those detachments, were responsible to the PJP commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what did the commander command? Was that a unit or was it some other component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, are you asking me about the detachment commander or the overall PJP commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused about the distinction between a unit and a detachment. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "unit," I'm using this in a general sense, generic sense. When I say "unit" I mean both company and detachment; it could mean either one of those. I am trying to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you can understand that we will need some more elaboration on the command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, in the Serbian -- there is some discrepancy in English obviously, since the English language does not distinguish between "komandir" and "komandant," both are interpreted as "commander," so this gives rise to some ambiguity. From the bottom level up, all the way up to the minister, what is the command structure of these PJP units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Your Honour. The structure was as follows. The basic units of the PJP units were platoons. These numbered up to 25 members. The platoons, as a rule, would comprise three squads of up to ten police members or less. Several platoons of the police, three to four, sometimes even six, would make up a PJP company. A PJP company had its commander and deputy commander. Several companies of the PJP would make up a PJP detachment. There was several such detachments. These detachments had their own command structure comprising the detachment commanders and his assistants. Their number was determined based on the size of a detachment in the sense of its strength. All of the police detachments would answer to one "komandant," the "komandant" of all PJP units, who is in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who did he answer to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: He answered personally to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a pleasure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to show how certain relationships worked within the police, can you tell us what the discrepancy was in the salary of a member of a PJP, for example, on the one hand, and the sort of salary that they would have received as a regular police officer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: For as long as members of the PJP units were carrying out the duties that were assigned to them, there was a discrepancy in relation to their regular salary, what it would have been, in the sense of an increase, the amount being no more than 0.42 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Paunovic, you can speak slowly but without the interruptions. The important thing is for us to make a pause between my questions and your answers, since we're using the same language. I know it's more difficult like this to interrupt your own train of thought.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there isn't a translation issue in line 2 of page 43, it is 0.42 per cent, is it, less than one-half per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was surprised as well. I clarified this with the witness before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 6D681 brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, have a look, please. Do we see there who is dispatching the PJP to Kosovo and Metohija on a mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, based on this document we can clearly see that the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, or rather, the minister who previously authorises these sector head is dispatching members of the PJP so that they might carry out security missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have, please, 6D682.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we look at this document, does it show who is dispatching PJP units to Kosovo and are there any discrepancies in relation to the previous document or does the procedure appear to be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure is entirely identical in terms of who dispatches the unit and who is responsible for it. I think the only difference between the two documents is their destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll not be opening up all the documents but just for the record the following documents were envisaged: 6D683, 6D684, 6D685, 6D686, 6D687, 6D291, and I think that should do, at least as far as this topic is concerned. Mr. Paunovic, based on what you know, how long were the shifts when units or parts of units were dispatched to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: The time a unit would spend on a security mission that it was dispatched to would depend on the nature of their mission. In most cases, however, it would be up to 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many police members were in Kosovo and Metohija after the signing of the agreement with the OSCE and before the start of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were informed by our superior officers of everything that was going on that had to do with our work and the way we went about our work. I remember that at the time there was the so-called Vienna Agreement which allowed for the presence of up to 10.000 policemen, that was before the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that agreement upheld? Was the figure mentioned complied with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were general instructions in an order from our superiors to uphold all the provisions and clauses of this international agreement and the commitments that we undertook. Therefore, as far as the area of responsibility of my unit was concerned, this was fully complied with. I assume the same situation prevailed in other units elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell us what your status was when, for example, you were sent on a mission as a PJP member?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of a PJP unit that was dispatched on a certain mission, my unit and other units were to provide support and assistance to whichever secretariat had territorial jurisdiction over a certain mission in the Ministry of the Interior whereby -- I mean the police. And they were entirely responsible for carrying out any missions in that particular area. We would, as a rule, be attached for better efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were sent to Kosovo in 1998, did the chief of the SUP in the territory where you were sent, was he in a position to issue any orders to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
utterances.text: I as the company "komandir" or deputy company "komandir," not, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But did it ever happen to you that you received any orders from the MUP staff, the MUP staff in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC
